paras.text: Business Management, Estimating, Finance, Personnel and Workers Comp — Audio Lecture

Welcome back. This chapter covers the biggest block of the Business and Law section of your Michigan Residential Builder exam. Out of fifty Business and Law questions, roughly nineteen come from this domain: six on project management and administration, six on accounting and finance, four on types of business organization, two on personnel, and one on estimating. Nail this chapter and you have banked more than a third of the Business and Law section. Let's go through it the way the exam thinks about it.

Start with business organization, because it is pure memorization and easy points. There are five structures you need to compare on two axes: liability and taxes. A sole proprietorship needs no state filing at all. It is the simplest structure, but the owner has unlimited personal liability — the house, the truck, the savings account, all of it is exposed. All profit lands on the owner's personal return and every dollar is hit with self employment tax. A general partnership is the same idea with two or more people, and it is worse than most people realize, because each partner has unlimited joint and several liability. That means a creditor can collect the entire partnership debt from any one partner, even a debt the other partner created. The L L C fixes the liability problem. You file Articles of Organization with LARA, and as long as you maintain the veil — separate bank accounts, no commingling, adequate capitalization, contracts signed in the company name — your personal assets are protected. Taxes pass through by default. Then there is the S corporation. Here is the trap: S corp status is not a Michigan filing. It is a federal election you make with the I R S on form twenty five fifty three. It gives you pass through taxation, but the owner who works in the business must take a reasonable W two salary. And finally the C corporation, which is the double taxation entity — the corporation pays tax on profits, and then shareholders pay tax again on dividends. Small builders almost never want it.

One housekeeping number for the L L C: the annual statement is due to LARA by February fifteenth every year, and the fee is twenty five dollars. Miss it for about two years and the company falls to not in good standing status. That status is restorable — the company does not automatically dissolve. That is a tested distinction.

Now accounting and finance. First, cash versus accrual. Cash basis records income when the money actually arrives and expenses when they are actually paid. Accrual records income when it is earned — when you bill it — and expenses when they are incurred. Accrual is what you need for real job costing, because it matches revenue to cost. For long term contracts, know the two revenue methods by name: percentage of completion, which recognizes revenue as the work progresses, and completed contract, which recognizes everything at the end.

Know your two financial statements cold. The balance sheet is a snapshot at a single point in time, and it is built on the accounting equation: assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity. Always. The income statement — the profit and loss — covers a period of time. Revenue minus direct job costs gives you gross profit. Gross profit minus overhead gives you net profit. If a question asks where the year's profit shows up, the answer is the income statement, not the balance sheet.

Here comes the one calculation I can almost promise you will see: markup versus margin. Markup is a percentage of cost. Margin is a percentage of the selling price. They are never the same number. Take a job that costs one hundred thousand dollars. Add a twenty five percent markup and you sell it for one hundred twenty five thousand. Your profit is twenty five thousand — but as a share of the sale price, that is only twenty percent. So a twenty five percent markup is a twenty percent margin. The famous ten and ten — ten percent overhead plus ten percent profit — is a twenty percent markup, and it produces only a sixteen point six seven percent margin. The formulas: margin equals markup divided by one plus markup. And if you want a target margin, divide cost by one minus the margin. To earn a twenty percent margin on an eighty thousand dollar job, you divide eighty thousand by point eight and price it at one hundred thousand. If you multiply by one point two instead, you just fell into the trap.

Two more money formulas. Overhead rate: total annual overhead divided by total annual direct costs. One hundred twenty six thousand of overhead against eight hundred forty thousand of direct cost is fifteen percent. And break even revenue: fixed overhead divided by gross margin percentage. One hundred fifty thousand of overhead at a thirty percent margin means you need five hundred thousand in revenue just to break even.

On cash flow, remember that contractors pay for labor and materials before the owner pays them. Accounts receivable is money owed to you; accounts payable is money you owe. A company with big receivables and no cash is profitable on paper and dying in real life. Underbilling means you have done more work than you have billed — you are financing the owner's project. Overbilling is the reverse. Bill promptly and match your billings to the work.

Billing runs on a schedule of values — the contract price broken into line items. The industry payment forms are A I A G seven zero two, the payment application summary, and G seven zero three, the line by line continuation sheet. Retainage is the five to ten percent the owner withholds from each draw until substantial or final completion, and Michigan has no statutory cap on it for private residential work. A lien safe draw schedule ties each draw to a completed milestone, and each check gets exchanged for a conditional lien waiver — conditional meaning it only takes effect when the payment clears. Never, ever sign an unconditional waiver before the money clears your bank, because an unconditional waiver is effective immediately whether you were paid or not.

Estimating next — light on the blueprint but the math is free money. Board feet: nominal thickness times nominal width times length in feet, divided by twelve. A two by six, ten feet long, is ten board feet. Concrete: length times width times thickness in feet gives cubic feet, and divide by twenty seven for cubic yards. A four inch slab, twenty four by thirty six feet, is two hundred eighty eight cubic feet, about ten point seven yards, call it twelve with waste. A roofing square is one hundred square feet. Waste factors: framing lumber ten to fifteen percent, drywall ten to twelve, shingles ten to fifteen, concrete five to ten, and engineered trusses essentially zero. Contingency is a risk reserve — five to ten percent on new construction, ten to twenty on remodels — and it goes into the estimate before overhead and profit, because it is not profit. Contract types: lump sum puts cost risk on the contractor and needs complete plans. Cost plus puts the risk on the owner and fits unknown scope, ideally with a not to exceed cap. Time and materials is hourly plus materials for small or undefined work. Unit price fits work where quantities are uncertain, like excavation. And an allowance is a plug number for something not yet selected; the difference gets settled by written change order — and in Michigan, every change order is in writing.

Project management. The critical path method: the critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks, and it sets the minimum project duration. Tasks on the critical path have zero float. Float, or slack, is how long a task can slip without moving the completion date. A Gantt chart — a bar chart — is the standard scheduling picture, but it does not inherently show dependencies; network diagrams do. Substantial completion means the owner can use the work for its intended purpose, and it triggers the punch list, the warranty clock, and release of most retainage. Final completion means everything, including the punch list, is done. Bonds come in three flavors: the bid bond guarantees you honor your bid, the performance bond guarantees you finish the work, and the payment bond guarantees your subs and suppliers get paid. When the exam asks which bond protects subcontractors, the answer is the payment bond.

Personnel and payroll. Employee versus independent contractor is decided by the I R S common law test — behavioral control, financial control, and the relationship of the parties — built on the twenty factors of revenue ruling eighty seven forty one. Michigan's workers comp statute adopted that exact twenty factor test for anything on or after January first, twenty thirteen. And if you withhold federal income tax for someone, that alone is prima facie evidence they are your employee. Payroll numbers: FICA is six point two percent social security plus one point four five percent medicare — seven point six five percent from the employer and the same from the employee. Federal unemployment, FUTA, is six percent of the first seven thousand dollars, but with the state credit it nets to point six percent. Withheld taxes are trust fund taxes, and owners are personally liable if they do not get remitted. Michigan unemployment through the U I A: the statutory default taxable wage base is nine thousand five hundred dollars, but it drops to nine thousand dollars for qualified employers — those with all reports filed and no unpaid balance — while the trust fund stays healthy, and nine thousand is the base that actually applies in twenty twenty five and twenty twenty six. Know both numbers. New employers pay two point seven percent — except construction. A new construction employer pays the average rate for the construction industry, which is several times higher. That exception is exactly the kind of thing this exam loves. One genuine change for twenty twenty six: the ten ninety nine reporting threshold rose from six hundred dollars to two thousand dollars for payments made this year. Older study materials still say six hundred. Overtime under the Fair Labor Standards Act is one and a half times the regular rate for hours over forty in a workweek — there is no federal daily overtime. And MIOSHA recordkeeping: employers with eleven or more employees keep the form three hundred injury log, post the annual summary from February first to April thirtieth, and keep records five years. Report a fatality within eight hours; report an in patient hospitalization, an amputation, or the loss of an eye within twenty four hours.

Workers compensation, Michigan style. The law is the Workers Disability Compensation Act, and it is administered by the Workers Disability Compensation Agency under the Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity — not LARA. It is a no fault system, and it is the exclusive remedy: the injured worker gets benefits — medical, wage loss, vocational rehab, death benefits — but cannot sue the employer. Coverage is required if you meet either of two triggers. Trigger one: you regularly employ three or more employees at one time, part timers included. Trigger two: even with fewer than three, if just one employee has worked thirty five or more hours a week for thirteen weeks or longer during the preceding fifty two weeks. Either one alone requires coverage. A sole proprietor with no employees is exempt but may opt in. Owners can be excluded by filing form W C three thirty seven: a corporate officer who owns at least ten percent of a corporation with ten or fewer stockholders, an L L C member manager who owns at least ten percent of an L L C with ten or fewer members, or a partner. Now the general contractor trap: if your sub has no workers comp and no valid exclusion on file, and his worker gets hurt on your site, the claim lands on you. Collect a comp certificate or the exclusion form before anyone swings a hammer. Penalties for going bare: it is a misdemeanor — up to one thousand dollars and up to six months, and every single day is a separate offense — plus the state can get a court injunction shutting you down and a civil fine of up to one thousand dollars per day, looking back three years. And an uninsured employer loses the exclusive remedy shield, meaning the injured worker can sue you in civil court. One more insurance term: the experience modification rate, or E M R. One point zero is average. Below one means a good safety record and cheaper premiums.

Time for the rapid fire recap. Michigan sales tax: six percent — contractor pays it on materials, labor is exempt, never charged on the contract price. L L C annual statement: February fifteenth, twenty five dollars. Markup to margin: twenty percent markup is sixteen point seven margin, twenty five markup is twenty margin, fifty markup is thirty three point three margin. Board feet: thickness times width times length over twelve. Concrete: cubic feet divided by twenty seven. Roofing square: one hundred square feet. Contingency: five to ten new, ten to twenty remodel, before profit. Retainage: five to ten percent. Workers comp triggers: three employees at one time, or one employee at thirty five hours for thirteen weeks in the last fifty two. Exclusion: form W C three thirty seven, ten or fewer owners, ten percent or more ownership. Penalty: a thousand dollars, six months, each day separate, plus a thousand a day civil. Independent contractor test: I R S twenty factors, since January first twenty thirteen. FICA: seven point six five each side. FUTA: point six percent net on seven thousand. U I A wage base: nine thousand five hundred statutory default, nine thousand for qualified employers right now; new construction employers pay the industry average, not two point seven. Ten ninety nine threshold: two thousand dollars starting this year. Overtime: time and a half over forty per week. MIOSHA: three hundred log at eleven employees, fatality in eight hours, hospitalization, amputation, or eye in twenty four. Payment bond pays the subs. Conditional waiver until the check clears. Assets equal liabilities plus equity.
That is the whole domain. Run the flashcards until the numbers come without thinking, and this block of the exam is yours.
